## Bar · Step 1 — Plain Bars {.smaller}

[Bar charts · build]{.eyebrow}

### 1 · Default matplotlib

Sort low-to-high so the largest bar ends on top, then draw. Functional, but every bar shouts equally and the frame is noisy.


<!-- slide 142 -->
## Bar · Step 2 — Colour Carries the Story {.smaller}

[Bar charts · build]{.eyebrow}

### 2 · One bold, the rest quiet

Build a colour list: red for Heart, grey for everything else. The eye lands on the one bar that matters before reading a single label.

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| code-line-numbers: "4,7"
#| output-location: column
#| fig-width: 6.2
#| fig-height: 4.4
from genomics_course.data import load_tissue_expression

te = load_tissue_expression().sort_values("tpm")              # tissue, tpm; sorted

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.2, 4.4))                    # one panel
ax.barh(te.tissue, te.tpm, color=colors)                      # apply the per-bar colours
ax.set_xlim(0, 100)                                           # zero baseline
plt.show()
```


<!-- slide 143 -->
## Bar · Step 3 — Drop the Frame {.smaller}

[Bar charts · build]{.eyebrow}

### 3 · Less ink

Hide the left, right, and top spines and the y-ticks, then add a faint grid on the x-axis only. Only the scale that matters survives.

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| code-line-numbers: "8-11"
#| output-location: column
#| fig-width: 6.2
#| fig-height: 4.4
from genomics_course.data import load_tissue_expression

te = load_tissue_expression().sort_values("tpm")              # tissue, tpm; sorted
colors = [RED if t == "Heart" else GREY for t in te.tissue]   # one bold, rest grey

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.2, 4.4))                    # one panel
ax.barh(te.tissue, te.tpm, color=colors)                      # coloured bars
for s in ["left", "right", "top"]:                            # walk the three unwanted spines
    ax.spines[s].set_visible(False)                           # remove each one
ax.tick_params(left=False)                                    # drop the y-axis tick marks
ax.grid(axis="x", alpha=.3, lw=.6); ax.set_axisbelow(True)    # faint x grid, behind the bars
ax.set_xlim(0, 100)                                           # zero baseline
plt.show()
```


<!-- slide 144 -->
## Bar · Step 4 — Label the Bars {.smaller}

[Bar charts · build]{.eyebrow}

### 4 · Values on the bars

`ax.bar_label` writes each value at the end of its bar. Now the reader gets the exact number without chasing a gridline.

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| code-line-numbers: "12"
#| output-location: column
#| fig-width: 6.2
#| fig-height: 4.4
from genomics_course.data import load_tissue_expression

te = load_tissue_expression().sort_values("tpm")              # tissue, tpm; sorted
colors = [RED if t == "Heart" else GREY for t in te.tissue]   # one bold, rest grey

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.2, 4.4))                    # one panel
ax.barh(te.tissue, te.tpm, color=colors)                      # coloured bars
for s in ["left", "right", "top"]:                            # remove unwanted spines
    ax.spines[s].set_visible(False)
ax.tick_params(left=False)                                    # no y ticks
ax.grid(axis="x", alpha=.3, lw=.6); ax.set_axisbelow(True)    # faint x grid behind bars
ax.bar_label(ax.containers[0], padding=6, color=INK, fontsize=10)  # value at the end of each bar
ax.set_xlim(0, 100)                                           # zero baseline
plt.show()
```


<!-- slide 145 -->
## Bar · Step 5 — Say What It Shows {.smaller}

[Bar charts · build]{.eyebrow}

### 5 · A descriptive title

A title that states the finding, not the variables. "BRCA1 is highest in heart tissue" does the interpreting for the reader; a subtitle gives the units.

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| code-line-numbers: "14-16"
#| output-location: column
#| fig-width: 6.2
#| fig-height: 4.4
from genomics_course.data import load_tissue_expression

te = load_tissue_expression().sort_values("tpm")              # tissue, tpm; sorted
colors = [RED if t == "Heart" else GREY for t in te.tissue]   # one bold, rest grey

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.2, 4.4))                    # one panel
ax.barh(te.tissue, te.tpm, color=colors)                      # coloured bars
for s in ["left", "right", "top"]:                            # remove unwanted spines
    ax.spines[s].set_visible(False)
ax.tick_params(left=False)                                    # no y ticks
ax.grid(axis="x", alpha=.3, lw=.6); ax.set_axisbelow(True)    # faint x grid behind bars
ax.bar_label(ax.containers[0], padding=6, color=INK, fontsize=10)  # value labels
ax.set_xlim(0, 100)                                           # zero baseline
fig.suptitle("BRCA1 is highest in heart tissue", fontsize=13, fontweight="bold",   # finding, not variables
             color=INK, x=.04, ha="left", y=.98)              # pin it left, near the top
fig.text(.04, .90, "Expression across five tissues (TPM)", fontsize=10, color=MUTED)  # subtitle = units
plt.tight_layout(rect=[0, 0, 1, .88])                         # leave headroom for the two-line header
plt.show()
```

::: {.takeaway}
[The bottom line]{.tl}
**Colour carries the story.** Spend the loud colour on the row that matters; frame, ticks, and legend disappear. The recipe: **sort → one bold colour → drop the frame → label the bars → title the finding.**
:::

<!-- slide 147 -->
## Stacked Bars · Composition Over Time {.smaller}

[Metagenomics · theory]{.eyebrow}

### Watch the whole shift, day by day

A stacked bar shows **composition**: each bar is a whole (one sample) split into parts (taxa) that sum to 1. Line the bars up **along time** and you don't just compare samples, you watch the community change: a perturbation hits, one taxon blooms, the rest recover.

Two rules keep it readable: keep the **taxon order and colours identical** across every bar, so a band means the same thing on day 1 and day 16, and mark the **event** (here, antibiotics) so the cause sits next to the effect. Microbiome tables arrive tidy/long, so the first move is a pivot to wide.


<!-- slide 148 -->
## Stacked Bars · The Data {.smaller}

[Metagenomics]{.eyebrow}

### Daily phylum abundance across an antibiotic course

`load_microbiome()` returns tidy long form: one row per day-taxon, abundances summing to 1 each day, with a `phase` label (baseline / antibiotic / recovery).

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| output-location: column
from genomics_course.data import load_microbiome

mb = load_microbiome()           # day, phase, taxon, abundance
mb.head(4)
```


<!-- slide 149 -->
## Stacked Bars · Step 1 — Pivot & Stack {.smaller}

[Metagenomics · build]{.eyebrow}

### 1 · Long to wide, stacked along time

Pivot to one row per day, one column per taxon, then stack the taxa with a running `bottom`. The x-axis is time, so the bloom is already visible mid-course.

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| code-line-numbers: "4,14-17"
#| output-location: column
#| fig-width: 6.8
#| fig-height: 4.4
from genomics_course.data import load_microbiome

mb = load_microbiome()                                            # long: day, phase, taxon, abundance
wide = mb.pivot(index="day", columns="taxon", values="abundance") # rows = days, columns = taxa
taxa = ["Firmicutes", "Bacteroidetes", "Proteobacteria",         # fixed taxon order for now
        "Actinobacteria", "Verrucomicrobia", "Other"]
tax_pal = {"Firmicutes": GREEN, "Bacteroidetes": BLUE,           # one fixed colour per taxon
           "Proteobacteria": RED, "Actinobacteria": AMBER,
           "Verrucomicrobia": PURPLE, "Other": GREY}
days = wide.index.values                                         # x positions = the days

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.8, 4.4))                       # one panel
bottom = np.zeros(len(wide))                                     # running base height of the stack
for t in taxa:                                                   # add one taxon layer at a time
    ax.bar(days, wide[t], bottom=bottom, color=tax_pal[t],       # this taxon's slice of each day
           width=1.0, linewidth=0, label=t)                      # width 1 so days touch into a band
    bottom += wide[t].values                                     # raise base for the next layer
ax.set_xlim(days.min() - 0.5, days.max() + 0.5)                  # tight x range
ax.set_ylim(0, 1)                                                # composition fills 0–1
ax.set_xlabel("day"); ax.set_ylabel("relative abundance")
plt.show()
```


<!-- slide 150 -->
## Stacked Bars · Step 2 — Order by Abundance {.smaller}

[Metagenomics · build]{.eyebrow}

### 2 · Most abundant at the bottom

Replace the fixed taxon list with one sorted by mean abundance. The dominant phyla anchor the base of every bar; rare ones ride on top, the convention that makes the stack legible.

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| code-line-numbers: "5-6"
#| output-location: column
#| fig-width: 6.8
#| fig-height: 4.4
from genomics_course.data import load_microbiome

mb = load_microbiome()                                           # long form
wide = mb.pivot(index="day", columns="taxon", values="abundance")  # days × taxa
taxa = (mb.groupby("taxon").abundance.mean()                     # mean abundance of each taxon...
          .sort_values(ascending=False).index)                  # ...most abundant first → stack bottom
tax_pal = {"Firmicutes": GREEN, "Bacteroidetes": BLUE,          # fixed colour per taxon
           "Proteobacteria": RED, "Actinobacteria": AMBER,
           "Verrucomicrobia": PURPLE, "Other": GREY}
days = wide.index.values                                         # days on x

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.8, 4.4))                       # one panel
bottom = np.zeros(len(wide))                                     # running base
for t in taxa:                                                  # layer in abundance order now
    ax.bar(days, wide[t], bottom=bottom, color=tax_pal[t],
           width=1.0, linewidth=0, label=t)
    bottom += wide[t].values                                     # raise base
ax.set_xlim(days.min() - 0.5, days.max() + 0.5)
ax.set_ylim(0, 1)
ax.set_xlabel("day"); ax.set_ylabel("relative abundance")
plt.show()
```


<!-- slide 151 -->
## Stacked Bars · Step 3 — Mark the Event {.smaller}

[Metagenomics · build]{.eyebrow}

### 3 · Put the cause next to the effect

Shade the antibiotic window and label it. Now the Proteobacteria swell sits directly under its trigger, the bloom reads as a *consequence*, not a coincidence.

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| code-line-numbers: "18-19"
#| output-location: column
#| fig-width: 6.8
#| fig-height: 4.4
from genomics_course.data import load_microbiome

mb = load_microbiome()                                           # long form
wide = mb.pivot(index="day", columns="taxon", values="abundance")  # days × taxa
taxa = (mb.groupby("taxon").abundance.mean()                     # taxa, most abundant first
          .sort_values(ascending=False).index)
tax_pal = {"Firmicutes": GREEN, "Bacteroidetes": BLUE,          # fixed colour per taxon
           "Proteobacteria": RED, "Actinobacteria": AMBER,
           "Verrucomicrobia": PURPLE, "Other": GREY}
days = wide.index.values

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.8, 4.4))
bottom = np.zeros(len(wide))
for t in taxa:                                                  # stack the taxa
    ax.bar(days, wide[t], bottom=bottom, color=tax_pal[t],
           width=1.0, linewidth=0, label=t)
    bottom += wide[t].values
ax.axvspan(4.5, 7.5, color=INK, alpha=.06)                       # shade the antibiotic window (days 5–7)
ax.text(6, 0.94, "antibiotics", ha="center", color=INK, fontsize=9)  # name the perturbation
ax.set_xlim(days.min() - 0.5, days.max() + 0.5)
ax.set_ylim(0, 1)
ax.set_xlabel("day"); ax.set_ylabel("relative abundance")
plt.show()
```


<!-- slide 152 -->
## Stacked Bars · Step 4 — Percent Axis & Finding {.smaller}

[Metagenomics · build]{.eyebrow}

### 4 · Name the result

Add the taxon legend, a percent y-axis, and a title that states the biology. The story reads in one glance: bloom under antibiotics, recovery after.

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| code-line-numbers: "1,22-23,25-28"
#| output-location: column
#| fig-width: 6.8
#| fig-height: 4.4
import matplotlib.ticker as mtick                                # percent-axis formatter
from genomics_course.data import load_microbiome

mb = load_microbiome()                                           # long form
wide = mb.pivot(index="day", columns="taxon", values="abundance")  # days × taxa
taxa = (mb.groupby("taxon").abundance.mean()                     # taxa, most abundant first
          .sort_values(ascending=False).index)
tax_pal = {"Firmicutes": GREEN, "Bacteroidetes": BLUE,          # fixed colour per taxon
           "Proteobacteria": RED, "Actinobacteria": AMBER,
           "Verrucomicrobia": PURPLE, "Other": GREY}
days = wide.index.values

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.8, 4.4))
bottom = np.zeros(len(wide))
for t in taxa:                                                  # stack the taxa
    ax.bar(days, wide[t], bottom=bottom, color=tax_pal[t],
           width=1.0, linewidth=0, label=t)
    bottom += wide[t].values
ax.axvspan(4.5, 7.5, color=INK, alpha=.06)                       # antibiotic window
ax.text(6, 0.94, "antibiotics", ha="center", color=INK, fontsize=9)
ax.set_xlim(days.min() - 0.5, days.max() + 0.5)
ax.set_ylim(0, 1); ax.set_yticks([0, .5, 1])                    # clean 0 / 50 / 100 ticks
ax.yaxis.set_major_formatter(mtick.PercentFormatter(1, decimals=0))  # render 0–1 as 0–100%
ax.set_xlabel("day"); ax.set_ylabel("relative abundance")
ax.set_title("ANTIBIOTICS TRIGGER A PROTEOBACTERIA BLOOM",       # title = the finding
             color="#333333", fontweight="bold", loc="left")
ax.legend(bbox_to_anchor=(1.01, 1), loc="upper left",            # taxon key, outside right
          frameon=False, fontsize=8)
plt.show()
```

::: {.takeaway}
[The bottom line]{.tl}
Along time, a stacked bar shows the community *moving*: **pivot to days×taxa → order taxa by abundance → mark the event → percent axis + finding**. Fixed colours and band order let the eye track one taxon across the whole course, the Proteobacteria bloom rises under antibiotics and fades in recovery.
:::

<!-- slide 154 -->
## Treemap · The Data {.smaller}

[Composition · treemap]{.eyebrow}

### Collapse time to one community

The stacked bar showed every day. Average across them and you get the whole community as one set of parts, exactly what a treemap wants.

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| output-location: column
from genomics_course.data import load_microbiome

mb = load_microbiome()                                          # day, phase, taxon, abundance
comm = (mb.groupby("taxon").abundance.mean()                    # mean abundance across all days
          .sort_values(ascending=False).reset_index())         # biggest first
comm["pct"] = comm.abundance * 100                             # as a percentage for labels
comm
```


<!-- slide 155 -->
## Treemap · Step 1 — Tile by Value {.smaller}

[Composition · build]{.eyebrow}

### 1 · squarify

`squarify.plot` takes sizes and labels and tiles them largest-first. `pad=True` leaves thin gaps so tiles read as separate. Turn the axis off, it's a canvas, not a plot.

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| code-line-numbers: "5,10-11"
#| output-location: column
#| fig-width: 6.2
#| fig-height: 5.0
import squarify                                                  # the treemap layout library
from genomics_course.data import load_microbiome

mb = load_microbiome()                                           # long form
comm = (mb.groupby("taxon").abundance.mean()                     # community = mean over all days
          .sort_values(ascending=False).reset_index())          # biggest first (squarify expects sorted)
comm["pct"] = comm.abundance * 100                              # percentages for the labels
labels = [f"{t}\n{p:.0f}%" for t, p in zip(comm.taxon, comm.pct)]  # "Firmicutes\n33%" per tile

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.2, 5.0)); ax.set_axis_off()   # blank canvas, no axes
squarify.plot(sizes=comm.abundance, label=labels, pad=True,     # tile area == abundance
              color=[GREEN, BLUE, RED, AMBER, PURPLE, GREY], ax=ax)  # explicit taxon colours
plt.show()
```


<!-- slide 156 -->
## Treemap · Step 2 — Palette from pypalettes {.smaller}

[Composition · build]{.eyebrow}

### 2 · Borrow a curated palette

`pypalettes` ships hundreds of named palettes. `load_cmap` fetches one; `pd.factorize` turns the category column into colour indices, so each taxon gets its own swatch. White label text reads cleanly on the darker tiles.

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| code-line-numbers: "2,10-12,16"
#| output-location: column
#| fig-width: 6.2
#| fig-height: 5.0
import squarify
from pypalettes import load_cmap                                 # curated palette library
from genomics_course.data import load_microbiome

mb = load_microbiome()                                           # long form
comm = (mb.groupby("taxon").abundance.mean()                     # community mean over days
          .sort_values(ascending=False).reset_index())
comm["pct"] = comm.abundance * 100                              # percentages
labels = [f"{t}\n{p:.0f}%" for t, p in zip(comm.taxon, comm.pct)]  # tile labels

cmap = load_cmap("Acadia")                                       # any named palette (discrete cmap)
codes, _ = pd.factorize(comm.taxon)                              # taxon → integer index 0,1,2,...
colors = [cmap(c) for c in codes]                                # one palette colour per taxon

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.2, 5.0)); ax.set_axis_off()   # blank canvas
squarify.plot(sizes=comm.abundance, label=labels, color=colors, pad=True,  # tiles in palette colours
              text_kwargs={"color": "white", "fontsize": 10}, ax=ax)       # white labels on the tiles
plt.show()
```

::: {.takeaway}
[The bottom line]{.tl}
A treemap shows part-to-whole when there are too many parts for a bar or pie. **squarify** tiles a flat set, sized by value; style it with any **pypalettes** colormap. Label the tiles, areas are read approximately, not precisely.
:::

<!-- slide 158 -->
## Admixture · The Data {.smaller}

[Population structure]{.eyebrow}

### One row per individual, ancestry split across K populations

`load_admixture()` returns each individual's inferred ancestry across five source populations (`K1`–`K5`, summing to 1) plus its assigned population. An admixture plot turns each row into one stacked bar.

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| output-location: column
from genomics_course.data import load_admixture

adm = load_admixture()   # individual, population, K1..K5
adm.head(4)
```


<!-- slide 159 -->
## Admixture · Step 1 — Stack the Components {.smaller}

[Population structure · build]{.eyebrow}

### 1 · Stacked bars

One bar per individual, each K segment stacked on the last via a running `bottom`. With `width=1.0` and `linewidth=0` the bars touch into a solid block. Within each population the order is still random, so it looks noisy.

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| code-line-numbers: "9-12"
#| output-location: column
#| fig-width: 6.0
#| fig-height: 4.4
from genomics_course.data import load_admixture

adm = load_admixture()                                            # individual, population, K1..K5
adm = adm.sample(frac=1, random_state=1).sort_values("population", kind="stable").reset_index(drop=True)  # shuffle within pops so sorting later has an effect
Kc = ["K1", "K2", "K3", "K4", "K5"]                               # the five ancestry columns
pal = [GREEN, BLUE, AMBER, RED, PURPLE]                           # one colour per ancestry

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.0, 4.4))                        # one panel
x = np.arange(len(adm)); bottom = np.zeros(len(adm))             # x = individuals, running stack base
for k, col in enumerate(Kc):                                      # stack one K component at a time
    ax.bar(x, adm[col], bottom=bottom, color=pal[k], width=1.0, linewidth=0, label=col)  # this K's slice
    bottom += adm[col].values                                     # raise base for the next K
ax.set_xlim(-0.5, len(adm) - 0.5); ax.set_ylim(0, 1)             # tight x, full 0–1 height
ax.set_ylabel("ancestry proportion")
plt.show()
```


<!-- slide 160 -->
## Admixture · Step 2 — Sort Within Population {.smaller}

[Population structure · build]{.eyebrow}

### 2 · Order

For each population, find its dominant ancestry and sort its individuals by that column. The noise resolves into a clean gradient, the single most important step for a readable admixture plot.

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| code-line-numbers: "8-13"
#| output-location: column
#| fig-width: 6.0
#| fig-height: 4.4
from genomics_course.data import load_admixture

adm = load_admixture()                                            # individual, population, K1..K5
adm = adm.sample(frac=1, random_state=1).sort_values("population", kind="stable").reset_index(drop=True)  # grouped by pop, shuffled within
Kc = ["K1", "K2", "K3", "K4", "K5"]                               # ancestry columns
pal = [GREEN, BLUE, AMBER, RED, PURPLE]                           # ancestry colours

parts = []                                                        # collect each sorted population block
for p in adm.population.drop_duplicates():                        # for each population, in order
    block = adm[adm.population == p]                              # just that population's individuals
    dom = block[Kc].mean().idxmax()                              # its dominant ancestry column
    parts.append(block.sort_values(dom, ascending=False))        # sort individuals by that ancestry
adm = pd.concat(parts, ignore_index=True)                        # stitch the sorted blocks back together

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.0, 4.4))                        # one panel
x = np.arange(len(adm)); bottom = np.zeros(len(adm))             # x = individuals, stack base
for k, col in enumerate(Kc):                                      # stack the K components
    ax.bar(x, adm[col], bottom=bottom, color=pal[k], width=1.0, linewidth=0, label=col)
    bottom += adm[col].values                                     # raise base
ax.set_xlim(-0.5, len(adm) - 0.5); ax.set_ylim(0, 1)
ax.set_ylabel("ancestry proportion")
plt.show()
```


<!-- slide 161 -->
## Admixture · Step 3 — Separate the Populations {.smaller}

[Population structure · build]{.eyebrow}

### 3 · White lines

Find where one population ends and the next begins (cumulative group sizes) and draw a thin white line at each boundary. Now the five groups read as distinct blocks.

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| code-line-numbers: "15-17,24-25"
#| output-location: column
#| fig-width: 6.0
#| fig-height: 4.4
from genomics_course.data import load_admixture

adm = load_admixture()                                            # individual, population, K1..K5
adm = adm.sample(frac=1, random_state=1).sort_values("population", kind="stable").reset_index(drop=True)
Kc = ["K1", "K2", "K3", "K4", "K5"]                               # ancestry columns
pal = [GREEN, BLUE, AMBER, RED, PURPLE]                           # ancestry colours

parts = []                                                        # sort within each population (as Step 2)
for p in adm.population.drop_duplicates():
    block = adm[adm.population == p]
    dom = block[Kc].mean().idxmax()
    parts.append(block.sort_values(dom, ascending=False))
adm = pd.concat(parts, ignore_index=True)

pops = adm.population.drop_duplicates().tolist()                  # populations in plotted order
sizes = adm.population.value_counts()[pops].values               # how many individuals in each
bounds = np.cumsum(sizes)                                         # cumulative edges between populations

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.0, 4.4))                        # one panel
x = np.arange(len(adm)); bottom = np.zeros(len(adm))
for k, col in enumerate(Kc):                                      # stack the K components
    ax.bar(x, adm[col], bottom=bottom, color=pal[k], width=1.0, linewidth=0, label=col)
    bottom += adm[col].values
for b in bounds[:-1]:                                             # at every internal boundary...
    ax.axvline(b - 0.5, color="white", lw=2.2)                   # ...draw a white separator
ax.set_xlim(-0.5, len(adm) - 0.5); ax.set_ylim(0, 1)
ax.set_ylabel("ancestry proportion")
plt.show()
```

## Admixture · Step 4 — Label & Polish {.smaller}

[Population structure · build]{.eyebrow}

### 4 · Read it

Put one tick at the centre of each population block, label it, add the K legend and a title. The figure now reads itself: who is mostly one ancestry, who is admixed.

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| code-line-numbers: "26-27,30-31"
#| output-location: column
#| fig-width: 6.0
#| fig-height: 4.4
from genomics_course.data import load_admixture

adm = load_admixture()                                            # individual, population, K1..K5
adm = adm.sample(frac=1, random_state=1).sort_values("population", kind="stable").reset_index(drop=True)
Kc = ["K1", "K2", "K3", "K4", "K5"]                               # ancestry columns
pal = [GREEN, BLUE, AMBER, RED, PURPLE]                           # ancestry colours

parts = []                                                        # sort within each population
for p in adm.population.drop_duplicates():
    block = adm[adm.population == p]
    dom = block[Kc].mean().idxmax()
    parts.append(block.sort_values(dom, ascending=False))
adm = pd.concat(parts, ignore_index=True)

pops = adm.population.drop_duplicates().tolist()                  # population order
sizes = adm.population.value_counts()[pops].values               # block sizes
bounds = np.cumsum(sizes)                                         # cumulative boundaries

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.0, 4.4))                        # one panel
x = np.arange(len(adm)); bottom = np.zeros(len(adm))
for k, col in enumerate(Kc):                                      # stack the K components
    ax.bar(x, adm[col], bottom=bottom, color=pal[k], width=1.0, linewidth=0, label=col)
    bottom += adm[col].values
for b in bounds[:-1]:                                             # white separators between populations
    ax.axvline(b - 0.5, color="white", lw=2.2)
ax.set_xticks(bounds - sizes / 2)                                # one tick at each block's centre
ax.set_xticklabels(pops, fontweight="bold", fontsize=9)          # label it with the population name
ax.set_xlim(-0.5, len(adm) - 0.5); ax.set_ylim(0, 1); ax.set_yticks([0, .5, 1])
ax.set_ylabel("ancestry proportion")
ax.set_title("ADMIXTURE — K=5 ancestry components", color="#333333", fontweight="bold", loc="left")  # title
ax.legend(title="K", bbox_to_anchor=(1.01, 1), loc="upper left", frameon=False, fontsize=8)  # K colour key
plt.show()
```

::: {.takeaway}
[The bottom line]{.tl}
Each bar is one individual, each segment an ancestry fraction. The recipe: **stack → sort within population → separate with white lines → label**. Sorting is what turns noise into structure, AMR shows the most admixture, the rest are largely single-ancestry.
:::

## Admixture · The Data {.smaller}

[Population structure]{.eyebrow}

### One row per individual, ancestry split across K populations

`load_admixture()` returns each individual's inferred ancestry across five source populations (`K1`–`K5`, summing to 1) plus its assigned population. An admixture plot turns each row into one stacked bar.

```{python}

adm.head(4)
```


<!-- slide 164 -->
## Admixture · Step 1 — Stack the Components {.smaller}

[Population structure · build]{.eyebrow}

### 1 · Stacked bars

One bar per individual, each K segment stacked on the last via a running `bottom`. With `width=1.0` and `linewidth=0` the bars touch into a solid block. Within each population the order is still random, so it looks noisy.

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| code-line-numbers: "9-12"
#| output-location: column
#| fig-width: 6.0
#| fig-height: 4.4
from genomics_course.data import load_admixture

adm = load_admixture()                                            # individual, population, K1..K5
adm = adm.sample(frac=1, random_state=1).sort_values("population", kind="stable").reset_index(drop=True)  # shuffle within pops so sorting later has an effect
Kc = ["K1", "K2", "K3", "K4", "K5"]                               # the five ancestry columns
pal = [GREEN, BLUE, AMBER, RED, PURPLE]                           # one colour per ancestry

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.0, 4.4))                        # one panel
x = np.arange(len(adm)); bottom = np.zeros(len(adm))             # x = individuals, running stack base
for k, col in enumerate(Kc):                                      # stack one K component at a time
    ax.bar(x, adm[col], bottom=bottom, color=pal[k], width=1.0, linewidth=0, label=col)  # this K's slice
    bottom += adm[col].values                                     # raise base for the next K
ax.set_xlim(-0.5, len(adm) - 0.5); ax.set_ylim(0, 1)             # tight x, full 0–1 height
ax.set_ylabel("ancestry proportion")
plt.show()
```


<!-- slide 165 -->
## Admixture · Step 2 — Sort Within Population {.smaller}

[Population structure · build]{.eyebrow}

### 2 · Order

For each population, find its dominant ancestry and sort its individuals by that column. The noise resolves into a clean gradient, the single most important step for a readable admixture plot.

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| code-line-numbers: "8-13"
#| output-location: column
#| fig-width: 6.0
#| fig-height: 4.4
from genomics_course.data import load_admixture

adm = load_admixture()                                            # individual, population, K1..K5
adm = adm.sample(frac=1, random_state=1).sort_values("population", kind="stable").reset_index(drop=True)  # grouped by pop, shuffled within
Kc = ["K1", "K2", "K3", "K4", "K5"]                               # ancestry columns
pal = [GREEN, BLUE, AMBER, RED, PURPLE]                           # ancestry colours

parts = []                                                        # collect each sorted population block
for p in adm.population.drop_duplicates():                        # for each population, in order
    block = adm[adm.population == p]                              # just that population's individuals
    dom = block[Kc].mean().idxmax()                              # its dominant ancestry column
    parts.append(block.sort_values(dom, ascending=False))        # sort individuals by that ancestry
adm = pd.concat(parts, ignore_index=True)                        # stitch the sorted blocks back together

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.0, 4.4))                        # one panel
x = np.arange(len(adm)); bottom = np.zeros(len(adm))             # x = individuals, stack base
for k, col in enumerate(Kc):                                      # stack the K components
    ax.bar(x, adm[col], bottom=bottom, color=pal[k], width=1.0, linewidth=0, label=col)
    bottom += adm[col].values                                     # raise base
ax.set_xlim(-0.5, len(adm) - 0.5); ax.set_ylim(0, 1)
ax.set_ylabel("ancestry proportion")
plt.show()
```
